Part I · Understand the project

1The project on one page#

A camera looks at every part. DefectSpotter answers three questions in about a tenth of a second: is this part unusual, where, and what should happen to it?

DefectSpotter is a visual inspection system for the end of a production line. It learns what good parts look like — from good parts only — and flags anything unusual. For every part it returns an anomaly score on an easy 0–100 scale, a heat map showing where the part looks unusual, and a three-way decision: ✓ PASS ship it, ⚠ CHECK let a human inspector decide, ✕ REJECT quarantine it. Not a single defect image is needed — neither to train the models nor to choose the decision thresholds.

data / imagesmodel or learned componentprocessing stepdecision / checkhumanstored files

The whole system in one picture. Lane 1 runs once per product (offline); lane 2 runs for every part in milliseconds; lane 3 keeps the system honest after deployment. Every box is explained in chapter 3 (flows) and chapters 4–14 (details).

What was built

  • Five anomaly detectors, all trained or built from good parts and calibrated the same way: PatchCore (deployed), a feature-space VAE and a pixel VAE (generative AI), a mean-image baseline and an ensemble — compared in chapter 10.
  • A label-free calibration: 0–100 score scale and cost-optimal PASS / CHECK / REJECT thresholds from held-out good parts and synthetic defects (procedural + Stable Diffusion).
  • Operations: camera-health gate, control charts, human review queue with audit log, lot re-qualification, few-shot onboarding of a new product.
  • A Gradio app (9 tabs, live demo last), a public API, a Colab notebook, a Hugging Face Space, tests and CI.

How to read this guide

  • Presenting it? Chapters 1, 2, 10, 17, then 18–19 (app tour and demo script).
  • Want the mechanics? Chapter 3 shows every flow step by step; chapters 6–13 explain each model and concept with its exact parameters.
  • Running it? Chapters 20–22.
  • Boxes labelled What is happening narrate a step; Why boxes justify a choice; In the code points to the file.
  • Use the search box (top left) to find a term — e.g. “KL”, “coreset”, “EWMA”.

2The problem#

Inspection is an economic decision under uncertainty: two kinds of mistakes with very different costs, plus a limited number of people.

A quality inspector at the end of a line must stop defective parts without throwing away good ones. Two errors cost money in opposite directions:

errorwhat happenstypical costhow DefectSpotter limits it
Escape (missed defect)a defective part passes and reaches the customer — complaint, return, warranty, recallhigh: 400 USD in this guide's scenarioa cost model that weighs escapes 200× more than a false reject
False rejecta good part is scrapped or reworkedlow per part: 2 USDa CHECK band: uncertain parts go to a human instead of the scrap bin
Human checkan inspector looks at a flagged part0.30 USD (36 s at 30 USD/h)only uncertain parts are sent; capacity is planned

Why a normal defect classifier is not enough

  • A classifier (“good / scratch / dent / …”) needs hundreds of labelled images per defect type. Defects are rare (≈1% of parts), so collecting them takes months.
  • New defect types appear (a new tool wears differently, a new supplier) — a classifier has never seen them and lets them pass.
  • Labelling pixel masks is expensive and inconsistent between people.

The turnaround: learn “normal”, flag the unusual

Anomaly detection models only the good parts, which every factory has in abundance. Anything that does not look like the good parts — whatever kind of defect it is — gets a high score. The price: the model cannot name the defect type, and anything unusual (including a dimmer lamp) looks suspicious; chapters 11–13 handle that.

Why three decisions and not two

Scores of good and defective parts overlap a little. Instead of forcing a guess in that overlap, a narrow CHECK band around the threshold routes uncertain parts to a human: cheaper than scrapping them, safer than shipping them. The band is sized so that inspectors are not overloaded (chapter 11).

The status quo DefectSpotter is compared with

100% manual inspection of 20,000 parts per 8-hour shift needs 25 inspectors, still misses 40 of 200 defects (people catch ≈ 80% of what they see) and costs about 22,000 USD per shift — see chapter 17.

3How it works — the flows#

What happens, in which order, from raw images to a decision on the line — and after deployment.

Six flows describe everything DefectSpotter does. Each diagram is followed by the same steps in words — what happens, in which order, and what comes out.

3.1Build flow — from raw images to deployable models#

processing stepstored filescomparison only

Seventeen stages in seven phases (python scripts/train.py --stages …). Phase 2 makes defects without any labels. Results are cached in ../defectspotter_work; the long stages are resumable per product.

  1. ≈ 1 minData — index, edaEvery MVTec image and mask is listed and split into four roles before anything is trained (no leakage). The EDA stage measures brightness, contrast, sharpness and defect sizes and draws the montages of chapter 4.
  2. ≈ 1 min (+ ≈ 4 min SD)Defects without labels — synthetic (+ optional diffusion script)Two synthetic defects are painted on every held-out good part (cut-paste, scratch or stain, each with an exact mask). Optionally generate_diffusion_defects.py refines 12 per product with Stable Diffusion.
  3. ≈ 70–90 minDetectors — patchcore, vae, fvae, meanPatchCore searches its per-product recipe on held-out good + synthetic defects and builds the memory bank; the two VAEs are trained from scratch on good parts; the baseline computes aligned mean/std images.
  4. ≈ 5 minStress sets — severity, diffusionEvery synthetic defect is replayed at 50% and 25% strength (the detection limit) and the diffusion defects are scored.
  5. ≈ 2 minCalibrate — calibrateFor every product × detector: 0–100 score scale, pixel scale, ensemble weight, capability check and the cost-optimal threshold and CHECK band. The ONNX backbone is exported and verified.
  6. ≈ 20 minEvaluate — evaluate, requalify, latency, drift, few_shotAll numbers of chapters 12–16 on held-out real defects: AUROC with bootstrap intervals, operating rates, lot-shift test, speed, drift stress test, new-product experiment.
  7. secondsPackage — examples, summarySample images for the app and reports/summary.json. The app reads only artifacts/, reports/ and examples/.
What is happening

Nothing in this flow looks at a real defect to make a choice. Real defects appear only in the evaluation phase, on images that never trained or calibrated anything. That is what makes the reported numbers an honest preview of a factory that has not seen its first defect yet.

3.2Inspection flow — one part, end to end#

data / imagesmodel or learned componentprocessing stepdecision / check

Ten steps, ≈ 84–136 ms per part on a 4-thread CPU. The dashed arrow is the camera-health override.

  1. Image inAny RGB image (camera, upload, API). It is kept at full resolution for the display.
  2. Camera-health checkBrightness, contrast and sharpness are compared with the qualified images as z-scores. |z| > 4 on any signal means the image is outside what the model was qualified on: whatever the model says, the part goes to CHECK with the message “check lamp / lens / camera”.
  3. Pose (screws only)The part mask (Otsu threshold on the colour distance to the background) gives the principal axis; the image is rotated so the screw lies horizontally, head on the left, centred.
  4. Resize + normaliseTo the product's resolution (224 px → 28 × 28 patches; 288 px → 36 × 36) and the ImageNet mean / standard deviation the backbone expects.
  5. screw 60 msBackboneThe frozen ResNet-18 (ONNX Runtime) computes layer2 and layer3 feature maps; layer3 is upsampled and concatenated: one 384-number descriptor per patch.
  6. screw 47 msNearest neighbourEvery patch descriptor is compared with the 1,309–3,318 vectors of the memory bank; the distance to the closest one is the patch's anomaly.
  7. Anomaly mapThe grid of distances is upsampled to the image, smoothed with a Gaussian and (screws) rotated back to the original pose; a pixel scale maps it to 0–100 (50 = more unusual than 99.9% of good pixels).
  8. Image scoreLargest patch distance (bottle) or mean of the top 1–5% of the map (screw, carpet), then mapped to 0–100: 25 = a typical good part, 75 = a typical synthetic defect.
  9. DecisionPASS below t − b, CHECK between, REJECT from t + b, with the product's calibrated threshold t and half-band b (or the lot's re-qualified ones).
  10. total 136 ms (median)ResultDecision card with the reason, the score bar, the heat map with numbered suspected regions (pixel score > 50), all detectors' opinions, a JSON record; CHECK parts can be sent to the review queue.
PatchCore timing per stage (reports/latency.csv). Screw is slower: 288 px input (36 × 36 patches) and pose normalisation. The total includes decoding, heat map and overlay rendering.

3.3Calibration flow — choosing thresholds without real defects#

data / imagesmodel or learned componentprocessing stepdecision / checkstored filescomparison only

From scores to a policy. Real defects (dashed) are scored the same way only to show how close the label-free threshold lands to the one labels would give.

  1. Score the calibration imagesHeld-out good parts (never seen by the model), synthetic defects at 100%, 50% and 25% strength and the diffusion defects go through the detector.
  2. Fit the 0–100 score scale25 = median raw score of the good parts, 75 = median of the synthetic defects; linear in between and beyond. Every detector and product now speaks the same language.
  3. Capability gateA defect set influences the threshold only if the detector separates it from good parts (AUROC ≥ 0.9). Faint 25% replays usually fail the gate — they mark the detection limit instead of dragging the threshold into the good parts.
  4. Cost searchEvery threshold 0–100 (step 0.5) × half-band {0, 2.5, …, 15} is priced with the cost model at 1% defects on kernel-smoothed score distributions; the band may use at most half the inspector capacity (5% of parts). The cheapest pair is the default policy.
  5. StoreEverything goes into artifacts/<product>/calibration.json: scales, policies, health reference, ensemble weight. The real-defect (“oracle”) threshold is computed the same way for comparison only.

3.4Human-in-the-loop flow — what happens to a CHECK#

decision / checkhumanstored files

Every CHECK is decided by a person and recorded.

  1. CHECKThe part's score is inside the band, or the camera was out of range.
  2. QueueBatch CHECKs are queued automatically; single inspections with “Send to review queue”.
  3. InspectThe inspector sees the part, the heat map, the score and the model decision; adds a note.
  4. Verdict“Confirm defect → REJECT” or “Release as good → PASS”.
  5. AuditTime, file, product, detector, score, threshold, model decision, verdict and note go into the audit log (downloadable CSV). Engineers review it; changes are deliberate releases, never automatic retraining.

3.5Monitoring and lot-change flow — after deployment#

data / imagesprocessing stepdecision / checkalarm / actionhumanmodel or learned component

Two different causes, two different fixes. A camera problem is fixed at the camera; a new lot is handled by re-qualification from good parts.

  1. Gate every imageCamera-health z-scores (|z| > 4 → CHECK).
  2. Chart the streamEWMA control charts (λ = 0.2, ±3σ, alarm after 2 consecutive points) on the score and on brightness / sharpness; the PSI compares this week's score histogram with qualification (< 0.1 stable, 0.1–0.25 watch, > 0.25 act).
  3. DiagnoseCamera signals moved → lamp, focus or position: fix it and re-verify on qualified parts. Only the scores of good parts moved → probably a new production lot.
  4. Test the lotInspect ~10 good parts of the current lot; a one-sided Mann–Whitney U test (p < 0.01) decides whether they score higher than the qualification's good parts.
  5. Re-qualifyIf yes: the new parts' patches join the memory bank (10% coreset), their leave-one-out scores become the good reference, synthetic defects are made from them and scale + threshold are re-fitted. Deployed as a recorded lot model (chapter 12).

3.6Deployment flow — from repository to users#

stored filesprocessing stepmodel or learned componenthumandata / images

One repository, three ways to run it.

  1. CommitCode, trained artifacts (≈ 57 MB) and reports live in the GitHub repository; GitHub Actions runs the tests on every push.
  2. Releasescripts/deploy_hf.py uploads the app, package, UI, artifacts, reports, examples and docs to the Hugging Face Space.
  3. ServeThe Space runs app.py (Gradio 6, ZeroGPU hardware; inference itself is CPU/ONNX). Users get the web UI and three API endpoints.
  4. ElsewhereThe same repository runs locally (python app.py) or in Colab; nothing needs a GPU or PyTorch at inference time.
Part II · Data and models

4The data#

Where the images come from, what they look like and how they are split.

MVTec AD (MVTec Software GmbH; Bergmann et al., IJCV 2021) is the standard benchmark for industrial anomaly detection: 5,354 high-resolution images of 15 products. Its training set contains only good parts — exactly the situation of a factory. The test set contains good parts and real defects, each defect with a pixel-accurate ground-truth mask. The project uses four products:

productwhy it was chosentrain (good)test goodtest defectivedefect types
bottleglass object, fixed top view — the “easy” case2092063broken large, broken small, contamination
screwsmall metal part at random orientation — the hard object32041119manipulated front, scratch head, scratch neck, thread side, thread top
carpetwoven texture — no object shape to rely on2802889color, cut, hole, metal contamination, thread
metal nutheld back as a new product for few-shot onboarding2202293bent, color, flip, scratch

Licence CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 (research and teaching, no commercial use). Downloaded from the Hugging Face mirror foersben/mvtec-ad pinned to revision c75b39616f84…, so every run gets byte-identical files (scripts/download_data.py).

4.1What the exploratory analysis showed#

  • Tiny defects dominate. Most defect masks cover less than 1% of the image — localisation metrics matter and down-scaling can hide defects (one reason screws use 288 px).
  • Acquisition is tightly controlled (small brightness / contrast spread). That makes good-only learning possible — and makes a lamp or focus change dangerous (chapter 13).
  • Test captures differ slightly from training captures. Carpet test images are brighter and come from a different roll; screw test images are darker. This “lot change” is real and is handled in chapter 12.
  • Test sets are ≈ 70% defective, unlike a real line (≈ 1%). All rates are therefore reported per class and costs are re-weighted to 1% defects.

Where defects occur (sum of all defect masks per product, reports/figures/eda_defect_location_*.png): bottle defects sit on the rim and inside; screw defects anywhere along the part; carpet defects anywhere.

4.2The leakage-free split#

data / imagesmodel or learned componentprocessing stepdecision / checkcomparison only

Four roles. The 20% of training goods held out for calibration play the part of “good parts the model has never seen”; the test set is split by defect type so both halves contain every type.

Why this matters

If the same images chose the threshold and measured it, the reported escape rate would be optimistic. Here the deployed thresholds come from ② + synthetic defects only, and every reported operating number comes from ④, which nothing ever saw before evaluation.

5Defects without labels#

Synthetic and diffusion-generated defects replace real defect images wherever a choice has to be made.

To choose a threshold you need to know what a defect's score looks like — but there are no defect images. The project paints its own defects on held-out good parts. They are not meant to look exactly like real defects; they only need to be unusual in a similar way (local, small, with a different texture or brightness).

5.2Severity replays — the detection limit#

Every synthetic defect is replayed at 50% and 25% strength (alpha-blended with the original). Full-strength defects are easy; the faint replays show where detection stops, like the minimum defect size in an inspection specification. They also make the recipe search meaningful (chapter 7): on full-strength defects alone every setting scores ≈ 1.0.

5.3Diffusion-refined defects (generative AI)#

A diffusion model generates images by learning to remove noise step by step. Stable Diffusion 1.5 with SDEdit (image-to-image: add partial noise — strength 0.45 — to a crop around a procedural defect and let the model denoise it, guided by a product-specific prompt) keeps the defect's position and shape but gives it photographic texture. An LCM-LoRA (a small low-rank adapter that distils the model to work in a handful of steps) makes this feasible on a CPU: 6 steps, guidance 1.5, ≈ 17 s per image. Only the masked region is composited back, so the rest of the part stays pixel-identical. 12 per product (4 per kind).

5.4Capability check — which defect sets may set the threshold#

A defect set only influences the default threshold if the detector can actually separate it from good parts (synthetic AUROC ≥ 0.9). 6The backbone: a frozen ResNet-18#

One pre-trained network turns every image into a grid of patch descriptors; it is never re-trained.

6.1Concepts#

  • Convolutional neural network (CNN). A stack of small learned filters slid over the image. Early layers respond to edges and colours, middle layers to textures and small shapes, deep layers to object parts. Each layer outputs a feature map: a grid in which every cell holds a vector describing the image patch under it.
  • ResNet. A CNN built from residual blocks that add their input to their output (y = x + F(x)). The shortcut lets very deep networks train. ResNet-18 has 18 weight layers in four stages (layer1– layer4, 64 / 128 / 256 / 512 channels); each stage halves the resolution (stride 4, 8, 16, 32).
  • Transfer learning. The weights come from ImageNet-1k (1.28 million everyday photos, 1,000 classes). Those generic visual features describe industrial surfaces remarkably well.
  • Frozen = not fine-tuned. Not a single backbone weight changes and no classification head is attached: there are no defect labels to train one, and fine-tuning on good parts alone could collapse the features. The backbone is a fixed “feature camera”.

6.2Exactly what is used#

itemvalue
weightstorchvision ResNet-18, ImageNet-1k
layers keptconv1 → layer1 → layer2 → layer3 — 2,782,784 parameters; layer4, global pooling and the classifier head are removed (too ImageNet-specific, not needed)
feature mapslayer2 (128 channels, stride 8 — fine texture) + layer3 (256 channels, stride 16 — object parts) upsampled to layer2's grid and concatenated → 384 numbers per patch
two outputspatch_features: 3 × 3 neighbourhood average (PatchCore's default, tolerant to tiny shifts) · patch_features_p1: raw descriptors (keep fine texture; all three deployed recipes use them)
input224 px → 28 × 28 grid, 288 px → 36 × 36 grid; ImageNet mean / std normalisation
exportONNX opset 17, dynamic batch and spatial size, 10.6 MB, verified against PyTorch (max abs error 2.4e-06)
runtimeONNX Runtime on CPU — the app needs neither PyTorch nor a GPU

6.3Why ResNet-18 — the backbone study#

PatchCore was run with four backbones at 224 px on the three products (scripts/backbone_study.py, analysis only):

Why

WideResNet-50 is slightly more accurate but its ONNX file is ≈ 95 MB and it is ≈ 2× slower. ResNet-18 is the most accurate backbone inside a 10–20 MB deployment budget, and the per-product recipe (chapter 7) closes most of the remaining gap.

7PatchCore — a memory of normal patches#

The deployed detector: no training by gradient descent, just a well-chosen memory of normal patches.

7.1The idea in one sentence#

A part is normal if every small patch of it looks like some patch of some good part. PatchCore (Roth et al., CVPR 2022) stores the patch descriptors of good parts in a memory bank and scores a new part by how far its patches are from their nearest stored neighbours.

data / imagesmodel or learned componentprocessing stepdecision / checkstored files

Build once, query for every part. Numbers are bottle / screw / carpet.

7.2The mathematics#

patch descriptor of a new part at grid cell (i, j): q_ij (384 numbers) memory bank: M = {{m_1, …, m_K}} patch anomaly: s_ij = min_k ‖ q_ij − m_k ‖₂ (Euclidean distance to the nearest normal patch) anomaly map: A = GaussianBlur( upsample(s), σ ) (σ = 2 or 4 px) image score: max_ij s_ij (score mode "max") mean of the largest k% of A (score mode "top-k", k = 1% or 5%)

The nearest-neighbour search is exact: distances are computed as ‖q‖² − 2 q·m + ‖m‖² in chunks of 8,192 bank vectors with NumPy matrix products — fast enough for a few thousand vectors without an index library.

7.3Coreset — a small bank that still covers everything#

Hundreds of good images × 784–1,296 patches = 130,928 / 331,776 / 175,616 vectors (bottle / screw / carpet). Searching all of them would be slow and the file large. A greedy k-center coreset keeps a small subset that still covers them:

selected = [random patch]
distance_to_selected = distance of every patch to it
repeat until K patches are selected:
    p = the patch with the largest distance_to_selected      # the least covered patch
    selected.append(p)
    distance_to_selected = min(distance_to_selected, distance to p)

Rare-but-normal details (a reflection seen in 2% of bottles) survive, because they are far from everything else — random subsampling would drop them. For speed, the distances inside the loop use a random Johnson–Lindenstrauss projection to 128 dimensions (which approximately preserves distances). Two engineering tricks: one greedy run serves every coreset ratio (its first K picks are the size-K coreset), and very large sets are first reduced to a random 300,000-vector candidate pool. Banks are stored in float16.

7.4The per-product recipe, chosen without labels#

Products differ: a bottle top needs a smooth view, carpet needs fine texture, screws need resolution and a canonical pose. Every combination below was tried per product and scored on held-out good parts + synthetic defects:

7.5Pose normalisation for screws#

CNN features are not rotation-invariant, and screws lie on the tray at any angle, so a memory bank would need every orientation of every thread. Classic machine vision fixes the pose first:

  1. MaskOtsu threshold on the colour distance to the background → the part's pixels.
  2. AxisPCA of the mask pixels: the first principal axis is the screw's long axis; elongation = √(λ₁/λ₂) ≈ 5–7 for screws, ≈ 1 for the round bottle top (never aligned).
  3. Head leftThe wider end (the head) is detected from the mask width at both ends and placed on the left.
  4. CentreThe part's extent (not its centroid, which sits near the heavy head) is moved to the image centre, so long screws are never cut off.
  5. RotateOne affine warp; corners are filled with the background colour. Rotation keeps the thread's handedness (a mirror flip would not).
  6. Warp backHeat maps are computed on the aligned image and warped back to the original frame (pixel-centre convention), so overlays and pixel metrics are unaffected.
Why it mattered

Screw image AUROC went from 0.935 (v1) to 0.983 with the per-product recipe (v2) to 0.997 with pose normalisation (v3); screw pixel AUROC 0.996.

In the code

defectspotter/patchcore.py (bank, coreset, scoring), defectspotter/pose.py, defectspotter/pipeline.py → stage_patchcore, _patchcore_search, _select_patchcore.

8Generative AI: variational autoencoders#

Two VAEs learn to rebuild good parts; whatever they cannot rebuild is suspicious.

8.1Autoencoders and VAEs — the concepts#

  • An autoencoder has an encoder that compresses the input into a small code (the latent) and a decoder that rebuilds the input from it. It is trained to make the reconstruction equal to the input.
  • Trained only on good parts, it learns to rebuild normal appearance. Shown a defect, it rebuilds what a good part would look like there — so the reconstruction error lights up where the defect is.
  • A variational autoencoder (VAE, Kingma & Welling 2014) makes the latent random: the encoder outputs a mean μ and a log-variance log σ² per latent number, and a sample z = μ + σ·ε with ε ~ N(0, 1) is decoded (the reparameterisation trick, which keeps the sampling differentiable).
  • A KL-divergence term keeps the latent distribution close to a standard normal. This regularises the code (smooth, no memorising of individual images) and makes the model generative — you could sample new good-looking parts.
loss = reconstruction error(x, x̂) + β · KL( q(z|x) ‖ N(0, I) ) KL = −½ · Σ ( 1 + log σ² − μ² − σ² ) (summed over latent numbers, averaged over the batch) β = 0.001 (small, so reconstructions stay sharp) at test time the mean μ is decoded (deterministic); the anomaly map is the reconstruction error
data / imagesmodel or learned componentprocessing stepdecision / check

Same idea, different inputs. The pixel VAE rebuilds 49,152 pixel values from 128 numbers; the feature VAE rebuilds the backbone's 384 × 28 × 28 descriptor grid from a 32 × 7 × 7 spatial latent.

8.2Pixel VAE (v1) — kept for comparison and for its reconstruction view#

itemvalue
inputRGB image resized to 128 × 128, values in [0, 1]
encoder4 stages of (stride-2 4 × 4 conv → GroupNorm → SiLU → 3 × 3 conv → GroupNorm → SiLU), 32 → 64 → 128 → 128 channels, 1 × 1 squeeze to 32 channels (8 × 8)
latent128 numbers (fully connected from the 32 × 8 × 8 map): μ and log σ²
decodermirror image with transposed convolutions, sigmoid output
lossL1 + 0.5 · (1 − SSIM) + 0.001 · KL — SSIM (structural similarity) compares local brightness, contrast and structure, so blurry averages are not rewarded
training120 epochs, AdamW (weight decay 1e-5), one-cycle learning rate up to 1e-3, batch 32; augmentation: horizontal flips (not for screws — it would mirror the thread), 90° rotations, ±4% brightness; best validation checkpoint kept
anomaly map0.5 · |input − reconstruction| + 0.5 · (1 − SSIM map), Gaussian σ 2; score = mean of the top 1%
size≈ 2 M parameters, 7.4 MB ONNX per product

Squeezing a whole image through 128 numbers gives a blurry average part: the error is large everywhere, so defects barely stand out (screw image AUROC 0.477 — no better than chance).

8.3Feature-space VAE (v3) — the generative detector#

The better VAE reconstructs what the backbone sees instead of raw pixels: the 384 × 28 × 28 grid of patch descriptors (224 px input, 3 × 3-averaged — the same features PatchCore uses).

itemvalue
inputbackbone feature map, normalised per channel with the training mean / std (std floored at 10% of the median channel std, so near-constant channels cannot explode the error)
encoder1 × 1 conv 384 → 256 · 3 × 3 stride-2 conv 256 → 128 (14 × 14) · 3 × 3 stride-2 conv 128 → 128 (7 × 7); GroupNorm + SiLU
latentspatial: 32 channels × 7 × 7 (μ and log σ² per position) — keeps where things are
decoder1 × 1 conv → two 4 × 4 stride-2 transposed convolutions back to 28 × 28 → 1 × 1 conv to 384 channels
lossmean-squared error on the normalised features + 0.001 · KL
training60 epochs, AdamW, one-cycle learning rate up to 2e-3, batch 16, feature-map flips (not for screws); best validation checkpoint kept
anomaly mapper-patch squared reconstruction error (computed inside the ONNX graph), upsampled, Gaussian σ 4; score = mean of the top 1%
size1.44 M parameters, 5.5 MB ONNX per product (+ the shared backbone)
productepochsbest validation losstraining minutes (CPU)
bottle600.08591.0
screw600.14681.5
carpet600.37661.4
Why the feature VAE works so much better

Descriptors are compact and semantic — a scratch is “unusual texture”, not thousands of changed pixel values — and the spatial latent keeps the layout. Normal patches are reconstructed accurately; defect patches, which the decoder never learned to produce, are not. Mean image AUROC: pixel VAE 0.683 → feature VAE 0.899. It still trails PatchCore on screws (0.798): a VAE generalises, so it partly rebuilds unusual thread patterns too, while a memory bank cannot.

8.4Ensemble#

ensemble score = w × PatchCore score + (1 − w) × feature-VAE score (both on the 0–100 scale)

w is chosen on held-out good parts + synthetic defects (full and 50% strength), scanning from PatchCore-only downwards so that ties keep the stronger single detector: w = 1.0 / 0.9 / 0.8 (bottle / screw / carpet). Chapter 10 shows it ties with PatchCore and is therefore not deployed.

defectspotter/vae.py, defectspotter/fvae.py; stages vae, fvae and the ensemble weight in stage_calibrate (defectspotter/pipeline.py).

9Classical baseline: the aligned mean image#

What a classical vision engineer would build first — the yardstick for the learned detectors.

The classical machine-vision reference: every image is aligned to a median good reference with OpenCV's ECC algorithm (enhanced correlation coefficient; none / translation / rigid / affine chosen on synthetic data), then compared pixel by pixel with the mean and standard deviation of the aligned good parts.

z(x, y) = | pixel(x, y) − mean(x, y) | / max( std(x, y), floor ) → Gaussian blur → score = mean of the top 1%
productalignment choseninputstd floorblur σimage AUROC

screwaffine224 px430.277
carpetnone224 px430.435
Why keep it

It is transparent, fast and needs no deep learning — and it shows exactly where learned features are needed: it works on the fixed bottle view but fails on rotating screws (a pixel-wise mean of rotated screws is a blur) and on textures, where every pixel varies.

10The five detectors compared#

All five were built and calibrated the same way — so they can be compared fairly. PatchCore wins.

Every entry of the app's Detector menu is a separate, fully built and calibrated model. Each learned only from good parts, got its own 0–100 score scale and its own label-free PASS / CHECK / REJECT thresholds, and is evaluated on the same held-out real defects. They differ in what they remember about a good part and how they measure “unusual”.

Verdict: PatchCore is the best detector and the deployed one

PatchCore has the best or tied-best image AUROC on every product (mean 0.979), the lowest expected cost (206 USD per 1,000 parts) and no false rejects at its label-free threshold. The ensemble is a statistical tie (mean 0.978; pixel metrics within 0.001) but runs two models (155 vs 88 ms) and costs slightly more (215 USD) — no benefit. Of the generative models the feature-space VAE (0.899) is far ahead of the pixel VAE (0.683). The mean-image baseline (0.562) shows why learned features are needed.

Part III · Decisions and operations

11From a score to a decision#

How a raw distance becomes PASS, CHECK or REJECT — with thresholds chosen without a single real defect.

11.1A common 0–100 score scale#

Raw scores mean nothing to an operator (a PatchCore distance of 2.7, a VAE error of 0.04 …). Every detector's score is mapped linearly so that 25 = the median held-out good part and 75 = the median synthetic defect:

score = 25 + 50 × (raw − median_good) / spread spread = max( median_synthetic − median_good, 4 × std_good )

11.3Choosing t and b: the cost model#

Every candidate (t, b) is priced as an expected cost per part at a realistic defect rate:

cost per part = (1 − p) · FRR · C_false_reject + p · escape_rate · C_escape + review_rate · C_check p = {cm['defect_prevalence']:g} (1% defective) C_escape = {cm['cost_escape']:g} C_false_reject = {cm['cost_false_reject']:g} C_check = {cm['cost_review']:g} (USD)
  • Grid: t from 0 to 100 in steps of 0.5; b ∈ {0, 2.5, 5, 7.5, 10, 12.5, 15}.
  • Smoothed rates. With ≈ 50 good parts a raw false-reject rate moves in 2% steps and the cheapest threshold sits right on top of one unlucky part. The rates are therefore read from kernel-density estimates of the score distributions (Gaussian kernels, Silverman's bandwidth, floor 0.5 points) — smooth and stable.
  • Capacity. The CHECK band may use at most 5% of the parts: 10% inspector capacity × 0.5 planning share — headroom for drift and new lots, as in any capacity planning.
  • Capability. Only defect sets the detector can see (AUROC ≥ 0.9, chapter 5.4) enter the defect side.

The app's Threshold & cost tab recomputes all of this live with your own numbers.

12New production lots: re-qualification#

When good parts of a new lot look different, update the reference of “good” — from good parts only.

A new production lot — another carpet roll, a new batch of screws, a different supplier's glass — can look slightly different while still being good. A good-only model then scores good parts higher and sends many of them to CHECK. That is exactly what MVTec's test images show for carpet: they come from a different roll than the training images, and the qualification model sent half of the good carpet parts to CHECK.

  1. CollectA handful (~10) of good parts of the current lot — no defects needed. On MVTec the good parts of the oracle split play this role; the operating split measures the effect.
  2. TestA one-sided Mann–Whitney U test asks: do these parts score higher than the qualification's held-out good parts? It compares ranks, so it needs no distribution assumption. p < 0.01 → lot change.
  3. Extend the memoryA 10% greedy coreset of the new parts' patches joins the memory bank — the old lot stays normal too.
  4. New good referenceEach new part is scored against the bank plus the other new parts (leave-one-out), so its own patches do not make it look perfect.
  5. Re-fitSynthetic defects are generated from the new parts; the score scale and the cost-optimal threshold are re-fitted exactly as in chapter 11.
  6. ReleaseThe lot model is stored with its date, source and test result; the app's Production lot switch selects it, and the API uses it by default.
productgood parts of current lotmedian score: lot vs qualificationp-valuetestdeployedgood parts sent to CHECKescapes
bottle724.2 vs 25.00.3846no changequalification model0.0% → 0.0%0.0% → 2.4%
screw1424.0 vs 25.00.8615no changequalification model0.0% → 0.0%6.4% → 1.3%
carpet1027.3 vs 25.00.0057lot changere-qualified model50.0% → 5.6%5.3% → 8.8%

For carpet, 10 good parts of the current lot added 784 patch vectors (10% coreset) to the bank; the re-fitted policy is threshold 39 ± 5. Shipped in artifacts/carpet/requalified/ and used by default for PatchCore.

Honest trade-off

Re-qualification removes most of the carpet CHECK load (49.6% → 5.7% of good parts), at the price of a few more escapes (5.3% → 8.8% on the operating split). Chapter 17 shows why that is the right trade on a real line: 12 inspectors per shift are not available, so the CHECK parts would not be looked at properly anyway.

A rule fixed in advance

For screw the test found no lot change (p = 0.86), so the qualification model stays deployed — even though re-qualifying would also have lowered its escapes on the test split. Choosing the model by its test result would be leakage.

13Monitoring and drift#

Keeping a good-only model honest after deployment: input validation, control charts, stability index.

A model that learned “normal” calls anything unusual a defect — including a dimmer lamp, a defocused lens or a bumped camera. Three mechanisms protect the line:

13.1Camera-health gate (every image)#

Brightness, contrast and sharpness of every image are compared with the qualified images:

z = (value − mean_qualified) / std_qualified any |z| > 4 → no automatic decision: PASS/REJECT become CHECK
Qualified reference (mean ± std of the model-training images, artifacts/<product>/calibration.json).

carpet90.4 ± 2.335.4 ± 1.73200.9 ± 329.7

Why CHECK and not REJECT? On an image the model was not qualified for, a REJECT is most likely a lighting false reject and a PASS could be an escape. A person decides, and the message says “check lamp / lens / camera”.

13.2Stress test: seven acquisition changes#

Every held-out good part was re-rendered with seven simulated changes at five severities. At full severity:

FR = good parts the model alone would REJECT; flagged = share caught by the health gate (then sent to CHECK). Changes the gate misses (camera shift, colour temperature) are caught by the control charts below.

15Metrics explained#

What each number in this guide and in the app means.

metricquestion it answershow it is computedgood value
Image AUROCAre defective parts ranked above good ones?probability that a random defective part scores higher than a random good part = area under the ROC curve; threshold-free1.0 (0.5 = guessing)
95% bootstrap intervalHow certain is the AUROC with ≈ 50–100 test images?resample the test set 1,000 times (stratified by class), 2.5th–97.5th percentilenarrow
ROC curveWhat does each threshold trade?true-positive rate (defects caught) vs false-positive rate (good flagged) as the threshold moveshugs the top-left
Average precision (AP)Ranking quality with many good partsarea under the precision–recall curve1.0
Pixel AUROCDoes the heat map light up on the defect?AUROC over pixels: ground-truth mask pixels vs normal pixels1.0
AUPRO @ 30%Are small defects localised as well as large ones?per-region overlap of the thresholded map with each defect region, averaged up to 30% false-positive pixels, normalised1.0
False-reject rateHow many good parts are scrapped?good parts → REJECT / good parts0%
Escape rateHow many defects ship?defective parts → PASS / defective parts0%
CHECK loadHow busy are the inspectors?share of all parts sent to CHECK, at 1% defects≤ 5%
Confusion matrixAll decisions at oncerows = truth (good / defective), columns = PASS / CHECK / REJECTdiagonal-ish
Expected cost / 1,000 partsWhat does the operating point cost?cost model of chapter 11 at 1% defectslow
LatencyCan it keep up with the line?end-to-end ms per part (median, p95) on a 4-thread CPU≪ cycle time
Why both kinds

AUROC measures the model (how well it separates); the operating rates measure the system (model + threshold + band). A detector can have a high AUROC and still behave badly if its threshold is chosen poorly — chapter 10 shows the pixel VAE rejecting 93% of good parts at its label-free threshold.

17Real-world numbers: one production shift#

Parts, people and money per shift — the language a plant manager speaks.

Rates are easier to judge as counts. The deployed operating points are turned into one 8-hour shift of a realistic inspection station (all values editable in the app's Threshold & cost tab):

assumptionvaluesource / reasoning
line speed2,500 parts/hour → 20,000 per shifta mid-speed station
defect rate1% → 200 defective parts per shifttypical first-pass yield
human check36 s → 100 checks per inspector-hourpick the part, look with the heat map, decide
inspector cost30 USD/hour → 0.30 USD per checkBLS median 22.82 USD/h (2024) + ~30% benefits and overhead
inspector hit rate80% of the defects they are shownindustry average (See 2015)
false reject2 USDvalue of a scrapped mid-value part
escape400 USD1-10-100 rule of cost of quality: a complaint ≈ 1,000× the inspection cost
One shift at the deployed thresholds (defectspotter/operations.py — the same numbers as the app's Overview).
productmodelparts to a humaninspectors neededdefects escapinggood parts scrappeddefects caughtcost per shift (USD)cost per year (USD)
bottledeployed PatchCore10 (0.0%)0.02.00198 of 200783195,854
screwdeployed PatchCore44 (0.2%)0.121.50178 of 2008,6282,157,115
carpettrained-lot model (before re-qualification)9,925 (49.6%)12.415.40185 of 2009,1532,288,202
carpetre-qualified for the current lot (deployed)1,132 (5.7%)1.423.90176 of 2009,8832,470,833
any100% manual inspection (status quo)20,000 (100.0%)25.040.00160 of 20022,0005,500,000
Was lowering the human workload right? Yes.

Before re-qualification carpet would have needed about 12.4 inspectors per shift; a station has 2–3, so most flagged parts would never be looked at properly (and an inspector who sees good parts all day stops looking carefully). Re-qualification brings it to 1.4. The honest price: about 8 more defective carpet sections escape per shift (24 instead of 15) — still far better than 100% manual inspection (25 inspectors, 40 escapes). A plant that can staff more inspectors raises Inspector capacity in the threshold lab; the CHECK band widens and buys those escapes back.

  • BLS Occupational Outlook Handbook — quality control inspectors, median pay 22.82 USD/hour (2024) — https://www.bls.gov/ooh/production/quality-control-inspectors.htm
  • See (2015), Visual inspection reliability for precision manufactured parts, Human Factors — industry-average hit rate ~80% — https://www.osti.gov/biblio/1236203
  • 1-10-100 rule of cost of quality — Labovitz, Chang & Rosansky, Making Quality Work (1992)

18The app, tab by tab#

What every page shows and how to use it.

The app is organised as a presentation: from the story (left) to the live demonstration (last tab). Every page starts with a box saying what you see and how to read it; every chart has a caption.

19Live demonstration#

What to click and upload, in which order, and what will happen.

19.1Three-minute script#

  1. OverviewThe problem (escapes vs false rejects), “learns only from good parts”, the eight indicators, the one-shift view.
  2. Inspect a defect🎬 Live demo → Inspect a part, product Bottle: upload demo_images/bottle/defect_broken_large_004.png → REJECT with the heat map on the break. Point at the score bar and the “Why?” text.
  3. Inspect a good partUpload demo_images/bottle/good_017.png → PASS.
  4. Hard caseProduct Screw: upload defect_scratch_head_009.png → the scratch is localised although screws lie at random angles (pose normalisation). Show “All detectors on this part”.
  5. ThresholdMove the threshold slider: the decision changes; ↺ restores the calibrated policy.

19.2Ten-minute script (adds operations)#

  1. Batch📦 Batch → Load sample batch → Inspect batch: tiles, score strip, CSV. CHECK parts land in the review queue.
  2. Review🧑‍🔧 Review queue: pick a pending part, write a note, confirm or release → audit log.
  3. Lamp failureUpload demo_images/drift_demo/bottle_good_part_lamp_failure.png: a good part under a failing lamp. The camera-health gate refuses an automatic decision → CHECK.
  4. New lot🌗 Drift & new lots → C: Load the sample current-lot good parts → Re-qualify (carpet). Good carpet parts that went to CHECK now PASS.
  5. Which model?📈 Results → Model comparison: five detectors, PatchCore best; the feature VAE is the best generative model.
  6. Money🎚️ Threshold & cost: change the escape cost or the line speed and watch the cost-optimal threshold move.

21Run, re-train, deploy#

Commands for every way of running the project.

21.1Use the live app#

Open huggingface.co/spaces/bhkr0901/defectspotter (direct: bhkr0901-defectspotter.hf.space). Nothing to install.

21.2Run it on your computer (CPU only)#

git clone https://github.com/hbasired/defectspotter.git
cd defectspotter
python -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate     # Windows: .venv\Scripts\activate
pip install -r requirements.txt                        # NumPy, OpenCV, ONNX Runtime, Gradio, Plotly
python app.py                                          # http://127.0.0.1:7860

The trained models (artifacts/), the evidence the app plots (reports/) and sample images (examples/) are in the repository, so the app works immediately — no GPU, no PyTorch.

21.3Re-train everything#

pip install -r requirements-train.txt                  # + PyTorch, torchvision, ONNX export
python scripts/download_data.py --dest data/mvtec_ad   # MVTec AD from the pinned Hugging Face mirror (1.3 GB)
python scripts/train.py --data data/mvtec_ad --stages index eda synthetic
pip install -r requirements-diffusion.txt              # optional: Stable Diffusion defects
python scripts/generate_diffusion_defects.py --data data/mvtec_ad --per-category 12
python scripts/train.py --data data/mvtec_ad --vae-epochs 120 \
       --stages patchcore vae fvae mean severity diffusion calibrate evaluate requalify latency drift few_shot examples summary
python scripts/summarize_results.py --write            # refresh result tables in README / handoff
python scripts/build_report.py                         # static HTML report
python scripts/make_demo_images.py                     # demo_images/ for presentations
python scripts/build_guide.py                          # this guide
pytest                                                 # tests

CPU ≈ 2–2.5 h on 4 cores (a GPU is ≈ 5× faster). Every stage caches its inputs in ../defectspotter_work; the long stages are resumable per product, so a single stage can be re-run after a change.

21.4Google Colab#

Open DefectSpotter_End_to_End_Colab_HUGGINGFACE.ipynb and run the cells top to bottom: it clones the repository, runs every stage with inline charts (including the five-detector comparison and the one-shift view), launches the app with a public link and can deploy to Hugging Face.

21.5Deploy to Hugging Face#

HF_TOKEN=<write token> python scripts/deploy_hf.py --space <user>/defectspotter

The script stages app.py, the defectspotter package, ui, artifacts, reports, examples and docs with a Space card, and uploads them. Details: DefectSpotter_HuggingFace_Deployment_Guide.md.

23Engineering decisions and lessons learned#

The problems met on the way and how each one was solved — useful when presenting “why it is built like this”.

problemcausefixeffect
Bottle picked an expensive recipe on noiseobjective differences of 0.001 decided between settingsparsimony rule: cheapest search within 0.005 of the bestsame accuracy, faster and smaller
Synthetic defects on the empty backgroundpercentile foreground mask leaked to the trayOtsu threshold on the colour distance to the backgrounddefects always on the part
Unstable thresholds≈ 50 good parts → false-reject rate in 2% stepskernel-smoothed rates (Silverman bandwidth)stable, reproducible thresholds
50% of parts to a human (carpet)the test captures come from another roll (lot change)planning share 0.5 of capacity + lot re-qualification from good partsCHECK 49.6% → 5.7% of good carpet parts
Screw escapes (≈ 9% in v2)random orientation; the bank had to cover every anglepose normalisation (PCA axis, head-left)screw AUROC 0.983 → 0.997
Long screw tips cut off after rotationcentring on the centroid (near the heavy head)centre the part's extent; pixel-centre warp conventionscrew pixel AUROC 0.996
Feature VAE error explodingnear-constant feature channels (std ≈ 0) divided by ≈ 0std floor at 10% of the median channel stdstable maps; verified on real features
Hours of coreset computationone greedy run per ratio and per candidate setCoresetLadder: one run serves all ratios; 300 k candidate poolrecipe search feasible on a CPU
Container restarts killed long runs2-hour limits and restarts in the build environmentresumable stages with done-markers and per-product cachesa restart costs minutes, not hours
Errors after a redeploya page opened before the update talks to a server with new event wiringbuild fingerprint + “reload” bannerno confusing errors after updates

24Responsible use and limitations#

What the system does not do, and the safeguards around it.

  • Human in the loop. Uncertain parts go to a person; every verdict is logged. The model is never silently retrained from verdicts.
  • No automatic decision on unqualified images. The camera-health gate turns PASS / REJECT into CHECK when the acquisition is out of range.
  • Thresholds chosen without real defects, measured on images that played no role in any choice.
  • The score is a ranking, not a probability. A score of 80 does not mean “80% defective”.
  • Heat maps show visual deviation, not root cause. A highlighted area is unusual; why it is unusual is for the inspector and the process engineer.
  • Synthetic defects do not cover every real failure mode. The detection-limit replays and the capability gate make this visible instead of hiding it.
  • Small test sets. 54–105 operating images per product — rates move in steps of 1–2%; AUROCs carry bootstrap intervals.
  • What the test set was used for. Design options (e.g. which backbones to compare) were proposed after looking at test results; the choice within the options is label-free. The backbone study is reported as analysis, not as selection evidence.
  • Licence. MVTec AD is CC BY-NC-SA 4.0: research and teaching only. A production system needs the plant's own images.

25Frequently asked questions#

Is the backbone fine-tuned?

No. ResNet-18 keeps its ImageNet weights; no head is attached.

So what is trained?

The memory bank is built from good parts (no gradients); the two VAEs are trained from scratch on good parts; the baseline computes statistics; the calibration fits a score scale and thresholds.

Did we build all five detectors?

Yes. All five are separate, calibrated models that can be selected in the app and the API; PatchCore is deployed because it is the best (chapter 10).

Were real defects used anywhere?

Only for evaluation and for the comparison “oracle” threshold — never to train a model or set the deployed threshold.

Why PASS / CHECK / REJECT and not good / bad?

Uncertain parts are cheaper to check than to scrap or ship; the band absorbs the overlap of the score distributions.

Why is the threshold not 50?

50 is just the middle of the scale. The cost model puts the threshold where the expected cost is lowest — usually in the high 30s, because an escape costs 200× a false reject.

What happens with a new lot or a camera change?

The health gate and the control charts raise an alarm; a camera problem is fixed at the camera, a new lot is re-qualified from ~10 good parts (chapters 12–13).

Can it name the defect type?

No — it finds the unusual area. Naming types would need labelled defects (a classifier on top of confirmed CHECK/REJECT parts is a natural next step).

Why ONNX?

One portable file per model, run by the light ONNX Runtime: no PyTorch, no GPU, identical results on a laptop, a Space or an industrial PC.

How fast is it?

84–136 ms per part with PatchCore on a 4-thread CPU, i.e. 440–710 parts per minute.

How big is it?

≈ 57 MB in total; the shared backbone is 10.6 MB and a product's bank 1–2.4 MB.

Why did I see errors after switching the detector?

The app had been updated while the page was open. Reload the page; the app now shows a reload banner in that case.

Can I add my own product?

Yes: 🆕 New product builds a model from a handful of good images; for production, run the pipeline on your own image folders.

26Glossary#

Anomaly detection
Learning what normal looks like and flagging deviations. → ch.
AP (average precision)
Area under the precision–recall curve. → ch.
AUPRO
Per-region overlap of the heat map with each defect, up to 30% false-positive pixels. → ch.
AUROC
Probability that a random defective part scores above a random good part. → ch.
Backbone
The pre-trained network that turns an image into features (here ResNet-18, frozen). → ch.
Band (CHECK band)
Half-width b around the threshold inside which parts go to a human. → ch.
Bootstrap interval
Uncertainty range from re-sampling the test set. → ch.
Calibration
Fitting the score scale and thresholds on held-out good parts + synthetic defects. → ch.
Capability gate
A defect set influences the threshold only if its AUROC ≥ 0.9. → ch.
CNN
Convolutional neural network: stacked learned filters. → ch.
Coreset (greedy k-center)
A small subset that covers a large set: repeatedly add the least-covered point. → ch.
Cost model
Expected cost per part from false rejects, escapes and checks at a defect rate. → ch.
CutPaste
Synthetic defect: a patch of the part pasted elsewhere. → ch.
Diffusion model
Generates images by removing noise step by step (Stable Diffusion). → ch.
ECC
Enhanced correlation coefficient image alignment (baseline). → ch.
Ensemble
Weighted mix of PatchCore and feature-VAE scores. → ch.
Escape
A defective part that is passed. → ch.
EWMA
Exponentially weighted moving average control chart. → ch.
False reject (FRR)
A good part that is rejected; FRR = rate. → ch.
Feature map / descriptor
The vector a CNN layer computes for each image patch (here 384 numbers). → ch.
Few-shot
Building a model from a handful of examples. → ch.
Frozen
Weights not changed during this project. → ch.
Health gate
Brightness / contrast / sharpness z-score check of every image. → ch.
Heat map (anomaly map)
Per-pixel anomaly score drawn over the image. → ch.
ImageNet
1.28 million labelled everyday photos used to pre-train the backbone. → ch.
Johnson–Lindenstrauss projection
Random projection to fewer dimensions that roughly preserves distances. → ch.
KDE
Kernel density estimate: a smooth estimate of a score distribution. → ch.
KL divergence
How different two probability distributions are; the VAE's regulariser. → ch.
Latent
The compressed code inside an autoencoder. → ch.
LCM-LoRA
Small adapter that lets Stable Diffusion work in ~6 steps. → ch.
Leave-one-out
Scoring each item with a model built from all the others. → ch.
Lot
A batch of production (roll, batch, supplier) that may look slightly different. → ch.
Mann–Whitney U
Rank test of whether one sample tends to be larger than another. → ch.
Memory bank
Stored patch descriptors of good parts (PatchCore). → ch.
MVTec AD
Industrial anomaly detection benchmark used here. → ch.
Nearest neighbour
The closest stored vector; its distance is the patch anomaly. → ch.
ONNX
Portable model format run by ONNX Runtime. → ch.
Oracle threshold
The threshold real defect labels would give — for comparison only. → ch.
PatchCore
Memory-bank anomaly detector (Roth et al. 2022) — the deployed detector. → ch.
Pose normalisation
Rotating each screw to a canonical orientation before feature extraction. → ch.
PSI
Population stability index of the score distribution. → ch.
Re-qualification
Updating the reference of “good” for a new lot from good parts. → ch.
Reparameterisation trick
z = μ + σ·ε, so sampling stays differentiable. → ch.
ResNet
CNN with residual (shortcut) connections. → ch.
SDEdit
Editing an image with a diffusion model by partial noising and denoising. → ch.
Score scale (0–100)
25 = typical good part, 75 = typical synthetic defect. → ch.
SSIM
Structural similarity index (brightness, contrast, structure). → ch.
Synthetic defect
A painted defect with an exact mask, used instead of real defects. → ch.
VAE
Variational autoencoder: an autoencoder with a random, regularised latent. → ch.
